item.title: Ethan Mollick：How do you picture a superintelligence (if true superintelligence could ever…
item.description:
How do you picture a superintelligence (if true superintelligence could ever be real)? I like a trick from Dungeons and Dragons for running villains with 25 Intelligence: don't try to out-plan the players. Instead, whatever they do or roll, play it like the big bad saw it coming.

item.description:
Yes! I think there is too much "we're so early" self-congratulation here. Many senior leaders in companies are smart, motivated, and understand a lot about their business. Many are also technically adept. They are absolutely getting AI. But changing a company is a longer process.

item.description:
They can use the channels built for humans, but which have far too much friction for any human to use. Your Clawlike is happy to navigate a phone tree or stay on hold or have an awkward conversation with an agent where they get rejected... and then try again.

item.title: emollick：Every firm's customer service agents are about to be overwhelmed with Dots & …
item.description:
Every firm's customer service agents are about to be overwhelmed with Dots & Muses & etc. negotiating for better deals using voice/chat. Stories of people delegating this sort of work to their agents & saving money as a result are popping up and are going to only go more viral.

Daron makes the argument for much more democratic input into the process, despite the many challenges that entails.

item.description:
Every one of the apps from the AI Labs have weird edges and are underdocumented and break sometimes and update without any sort of notice or changelog and change UIs on a dime...

... but the models behind them are really good and so everyone just shrugs and keeps on using them.

item.description:
A broken early version of whatever product they are shipping is still better then what a well-built traditional product a lot of the time because LLMs are just unreasonably effective tools at doing a vast array of stuff and people & companies are learning to just roll with it.

item.description:
It does feel like every year OpenAI releases a variation on the same third-party ecosystem only to semi-abandon it: Plugins in 2023, GPTs and the GPT Store in 2023-2024, Apps in 2025, and now Plugins (same name, different thing than before) in 2026.

item.description:
It also has a natural analog on teams as a persistent entity with a job that you can delegate to using existing team communication tools like Slack. I expect more Clawlikes soon, though I don’t think they are the final form of this type of AI.

item.description:
I only used Dots briefly before launch, so can’t offer a detailed review, but I found it to be good & very much in the rapidly-expanding Clawlike category with Muse & Grokbot. Using a capable model with access to your data as an assistant & second opinion is remarkably useful.

item.title: emollick：The impact of AI on jobs is still pretty unclear at this point. I don't find this…
item.description:
The impact of AI on jobs is still pretty unclear at this point. I don't find this very surprising, as employers are still figuring out individual adoption, let alone how you use AI in complex organizations. Things may start to happen faster as agents capable of real work spread.

item.description:
In a world where cloud-based Clawlike assistants that give powerful models virtual computers are increasingly looking like the way forward for personal AI, it really does seem to suggest the choices Apple made for Siri (on-device, limited capabilities) may be the wrong direction.
